questions.question: In Exercise 0, running the sync against the real `dim_customers` mart twice in a row with no data changes produces 'Synced: 18 | Errors: 0' both times. What property does this demonstrate?
options: The sync is using a full sync strategy
The sync is idempotent — re-running it does not create duplicate or double-updated records
The sync failed silently both times
DuckDB caches query results, so the second run didn't actually execute
questions.explanation: Idempotency means re-running the same sync with unchanged data produces the same result with no side effects like duplicate records. The lesson explicitly contrasts this with a real CRM using INSERT instead of UPSERT, which would create 18 duplicate records on the second run.

questions.question: In the lesson's `reverse_etl_sync` mock, what specific problem does the bare `except Exception:` block create, as demonstrated by the Exercise 0 failure test (changing match_field to a nonexistent column)?
options: It causes the function to crash instead of completing
It catches the resulting KeyError and silently increments the error count for every row, reporting 'Synced: 0 | Errors: 18' with no detail about which exception occurred or why
It automatically retries the sync with a corrected match_field
It has no effect — the sync still succeeds
questions.explanation: The bare except Exception catches any error identically, including a KeyError from a bad match_field, and reports only a count (Synced: 0 | Errors: 18) with no logged detail. Production code should catch specific exceptions and log enough context to diagnose the actual cause.

questions.question: A Reverse ETL sync pushes warehouse data to Salesforce, but a CSM also manually edits one of the synced fields directly in Salesforce. What governance decision does this scenario require, according to the Coverage section?
options: Reverse ETL tools always prevent any manual edits in the destination
A documented conflict-resolution rule (warehouse wins vs. destination wins) per field, since the two values will conflict on the next sync
This scenario is impossible because Reverse ETL only writes to brand-new fields
The sync should be paused permanently once any manual edit occurs
questions.explanation: The Coverage section names conflict resolution explicitly: if a destination value is manually edited, the next sync must have a documented rule for which value wins. 'Warehouse always wins' risks overwriting legitimate manual corrections; 'destination wins' means the curated warehouse value never reliably reaches that field.

questions.question: Why does `extras/metrics_layer_example.yml` model a hypothetical 'BrightCart+' subscription tier instead of using BrightCart's actual seeded order data directly?
options: Subscription metrics cannot be expressed in MetricFlow YAML

BrightCart's seeded data (`sample_dbt_project`) is one-off e-commerce orders, not subscriptions, so MRR/ARPU concepts require a different (hypothetical) fct_subscriptions mart to demonstrate the semantic-model pattern
The file is randomly generated and unrelated to BrightCart
MRR only applies to companies with zero one-off orders
questions.explanation: BrightCart's real seed data models one-off orders, which have no natural 'monthly recurring revenue.' The metrics_layer_example.yml file documents the semantic-model/metrics pattern against a hypothetical subscription tier and fct_subscriptions mart, explicitly noting it's a reference fixture, not a model that runs against the existing seed data.

questions.question: What does it mean to 'version' a metric like total_mrr rather than silently redefining it?
options: Versioning means deleting the old metric definition immediately once a new one is needed

Versioning means creating a distinct name (e.g., total_mrr_v2) or coordinating a single communicated cutover, so historical dashboards built on the old definition don't silently show different numbers with no warning
Versioning only applies to dbt models, never to metrics
Metrics cannot be versioned; only models can
questions.explanation: Silently changing a metric's definition (e.g., to exclude a new plan type) breaks trust in historical dashboards without warning. The lesson's governance coverage recommends explicit versioning or a coordinated, communicated cutover instead of a silent redefinition.

questions.question: Per the Build vs. Buy decision guide, when is building a custom Reverse ETL script favored over buying a tool like Hightouch or Census?
options: Always — custom scripts are universally cheaper
When there is small scope: 1-2 destinations and low row volume, where per-row vendor pricing may be overkill for a single low-volume sync
Only when syncing PII data, which vendors are never allowed to touch
Never — buying is always correct regardless of scale
questions.explanation: The decision guide favors building for small scope (1-2 destinations, low volume) where a scheduled script with proper idempotency/retry logic can work without vendor cost. Buying becomes favored as destinations multiply or schemas change frequently, due to the maintenance burden of custom code.

questions.question: Why must a semantic layer's cache TTL be shorter than the underlying data's freshness SLA, rather than longer?
options: Cache TTL has no relationship to freshness SLA
A stale cache showing yesterday's MRR as if it were live data recreates the exact 'which number is right' trust problem the semantic layer exists to solve
Longer cache TTLs are always preferred for performance regardless of staleness
Caching is incompatible with semantic layers entirely
questions.explanation: If a semantic layer caches results longer than the data's actual freshness SLA, a dashboard can show outdated numbers presented as current — the same metric-distrust problem (different numbers for the same metric) that a semantic layer is built to eliminate.

questions.question: Why does the 'Phase 7 Complete!' banner appear at the end of Day 84C specifically, rather than at the end of Day 84 or Day 84B?
options: It is a copy-paste error and should be removed
Phase_Overview.md's frontmatter lists 84C last in its days: sequence, confirming Day 84C is the actual final lesson of Phase 7's daily content
Day 84C is the first lesson in Phase 7, so it makes sense to mark completion there
The banner appears identically at the end of all three lessons (84, 84B, 84C)
